source_refs.note: Cardiac Cycle: Heartbeat: a main subheading of 11.1 Structure and functioning of the heart, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 237-238.

blocks.text: Heart works in continuous cycles. Its chambers relax and are passively filled with blood from large veins. Then, its chambers contract and propel the blood throughout body. Its alternating relaxations and contractions are collectively called a cardiac cycle or one heartbeat.

While atria are relaxed and being filled with blood, the ventricles are also relaxed. This relaxed period of heart chambers is called diastole. During diastole, both atria are filled with blood. As blood accumulates in atria, their blood pressure rises, due to which both of them contract. This is called atrial systole. It passes the blood through tricuspid and bicuspid valves into the two relaxed ventricles. When ventricles are filled with blood, both of them contract. This is called ventricular systole and it pumps the blood to pulmonary arteries and aorta. During ventricular systole, tricuspid and bicuspid valves close while pulmonary and aortic valves open.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Heart muscle is myogenic: the atria do not contract because filling raises their pressure. Each beat starts when the SA node (pacemaker) sends out an impulse; it spreads over both atria and they contract together. This is atrial systole.

In one complete heartbeat, diastole lasts about 0.4 sec, atrial systole takes about 0.1 sec, and the ventricular systole lasts about 0.3 sec. In one’s life, heart beats about 2.5 billion times, without stopping.

blocks.alt: Three small hearts arranged round a circle and joined by curved arrows: diastole (all chambers relaxed, 0.4 second) leads to atrial systole (atria contracting, shown dark red, 0.1 second), which leads to ventricular systole (ventricles contracting, 0.3 second), which leads back to diastole.
